questions.question: In the structural organization of eukaryotic chromatin, what is a 'Nucleosome' composed of?

options.A: Approximately 146 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octamer of core histone proteins ($2 \times H2A, H2B, H3, H4$)
options.B: A single linear strand of ribosomal RNA
options.D: A triplet codon bound to a tRNA anticodon

questions.explanation: A nucleosome consists of a histone octamer wrapped by ~146 bp of DNA, forming the fundamental 'beads-on-a-string' chromatin unit.

questions.question: Which histone protein acts as the linker histone (binding entry and exit DNA) to seal the nucleosome and facilitate 30-nm chromatin fiber compaction?

options.A: Histone H1

questions.explanation: Histone H1 is the linker histone that clamps DNA to the core octamer, promoting folding into denser 30-nm chromatin fibers.

questions.question: What distinguishes transcriptionally active 'Euchromatin' from transcriptionally silent 'Heterochromatin'?

options.A: Euchromatin is lightly packed and accessible to RNA polymerases, while heterochromatin is densely condensed and transcriptionally repressed
options.B: Euchromatin contains only RNA, while heterochromatin contains DNA
options.C: Heterochromatin is only found in bacterial plasmids

questions.explanation: Euchromatin is loosely coiled and active in gene expression, whereas heterochromatin (centromeres, telomeres, Barr body) is tightly condensed and silenced.

questions.question: Which landmark experiment by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) definitively proved that DNA (and not protein) is the genetic material of T2 bacteriophages?

options.A: Labeling phage DNA with radioactive Phosphorus-32 ($^{32}P$) and phage protein with radioactive Sulfur-35 ($^{35}S$)
options.B: Treating mice with heat-killed S-strain Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.C: Using X-ray crystallography on crystallized myoglobin
options.D: Culturing E. coli in heavy Nitrogen-15

questions.explanation: Hershey and Chase demonstrated that only $^{32}P$-labeled DNA entered bacterial cells to direct viral replication, confirming DNA as the genetic material.

questions.question: According to Chargaff's Rules for double-stranded DNA, which equimolar relationship always holds true?

options.A: $[A] = [T]$ and $[G] = [C]$, hence $[A + G] = [T + C]$ (Purines = Pyrimidines)

questions.explanation: Erwin Chargaff showed that in double-stranded DNA, Adenine pairs with Thymine ($A=T$) and Guanine pairs with Cytosine ($G \equiv C$).

questions.question: How many hydrogen bonds connect an Adenine-Thymine ($A-T$) pair and a Guanine-Cytosine ($G-C$) pair in double-stranded B-DNA?

options.A: 2 hydrogen bonds between $A-T$, and 3 hydrogen bonds between $G-C$
options.C: 1 hydrogen bond between each base pair

questions.explanation: Adenine and Thymine form 2 hydrogen bonds ($A=T$); Guanine and Cytosine form 3 hydrogen bonds ($G \equiv C$), conferring higher thermal stability.

questions.question: What is the antiparallel orientation of the two complementary strands in a double-stranded DNA molecule?

options.A: One strand runs $5' \rightarrow 3'$ while the complementary strand runs $3' \rightarrow 5'$
options.B: Both strands run in the same $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction
options.C: Both strands run in the same $3' \rightarrow 5'$ direction
options.D: Strands alternate direction every single codon

questions.explanation: The phosphodiester backbones run in opposite directions ($5' \rightarrow 3'$ paired with $3' \rightarrow 5'$), orienting complementary bases toward the central helix.

questions.question: Which historic experiment by Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl (1958) using isotope density gradient centrifugation proved that DNA replication is Semiconservative?

options.A: Growing E. coli in heavy $^{15}N$ isotope and chasing in light $^{14}N$ medium
options.C: Crystallizing calf thymus DNA with X-rays

questions.explanation: Meselson and Stahl observed a hybrid $^{15}N/^{14}N$ band in Generation 1, disproving conservative and dispersive models in favor of semiconservative replication.

questions.question: Which enzyme unwinds the double helix at the replication fork by breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs?

options.A: DNA Helicase

questions.explanation: DNA helicase moves along the DNA backbone, utilizing ATP hydrolysis to unwind the double helix and separate parental strands.

questions.question: Which enzyme relieves torsional strain and positive supercoiling ahead of the advancing replication fork by making transient cuts in DNA?

options.A: DNA Topoisomerase (DNA Gyrase)

questions.explanation: Topoisomerase cleaves and swivels phosphodiester bonds to relieve supercoiling generated by helicase unwinding.

questions.question: Why does DNA replication require an RNA primer synthesized by DNA Primase?

options.A: DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo; they can only attach new deoxynucleotides to a pre-existing free 3'-OH group
options.B: DNA polymerase cannot recognize thymine without RNA
options.C: RNA primers provide ATP to the helicase motor
options.D: RNA primers seal the sugar-phosphate backbone

questions.explanation: DNA polymerases require a free 3'-OH group to form phosphodiester bonds, provided by a short RNA primer laid down by primase.

questions.question: In what direction does DNA Polymerase synthesize all new DNA strands?

options.A: Exclusively in the $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction

questions.explanation: All known DNA polymerases read templates in the $3' \rightarrow 5'$ direction and synthesize the nascent strand strictly from $5' \rightarrow 3'$.

questions.question: What is the 'Lagging Strand' in DNA replication, and how is it synthesized?

options.A: The strand synthesized discontinuously away from the replication fork as short fragments called Okazaki Fragments
options.B: The strand synthesized continuously toward the replication fork
options.C: A strand composed entirely of ribosomal RNA
options.D: A strand that is never replicated

questions.explanation: Because replication is antiparallel and restricted to $5' \rightarrow 3'$, the lagging strand is built in discontinuous Okazaki fragments.

questions.question: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments together on the lagging strand by catalyzing the formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds?

options.A: DNA Ligase

questions.explanation: DNA ligase catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation between adjacent 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate nicks, completing strand continuity.

questions.question: In prokaryotes (like E. coli), which enzyme is the primary catalytic replicase responsible for synthesizing both leading and lagging strands?

options.A: DNA Polymerase III

questions.explanation: DNA Polymerase III is the main replicative enzyme in E. coli, possessing high processivity and $3' \rightarrow 5'$ proofreading exonuclease activity.

questions.question: Which prokaryotic enzyme removes RNA primers using its $5' \rightarrow 3'$ exonuclease activity and fills the resulting gaps with DNA nucleotides?

options.A: DNA Polymerase I

questions.explanation: DNA Polymerase I uses its unique $5' \rightarrow 3'$ exonuclease activity to degrade RNA primers (nick translation) and replace them with DNA.

questions.question: What is the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology formulated by Francis Crick?

options.A: DNA $\xrightarrow{\text{Transcription}}$ RNA $\xrightarrow{\text{Translation}}$ Protein

questions.explanation: The Central Dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA (replication) to messenger RNA (transcription) to protein synthesis (translation).

questions.question: Which enzyme transcribes genetic information from a DNA template strand into complementary Messenger RNA (mRNA)?

options.A: RNA Polymerase

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds to promoter regions on DNA, uncoils the template, and synthesizes complementary single-stranded RNA.

questions.question: What is a 'Promoter' region on a gene?

options.A: A specific DNA sequence (e.g., TATA box, Pribnow box) upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription
options.B: The stop codon terminating protein synthesis
options.C: A protein that destroys foreign DNA

questions.explanation: Promoters (like the TATA box in eukaryotes or $-10/-35$ consensus in prokaryotes) provide binding sites for transcription factors and RNA polymerase.

questions.question: In eukaryotic mRNA processing, what modifications are added to the primary transcript (pre-mRNA) before it exits the nucleus?

options.A: A 5' 7-methylguanosine cap, a 3' Poly-A tail, and RNA Splicing to remove non-coding introns
options.C: Addition of a phospholipid bilayer around the RNA

questions.explanation: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA undergoes 5' capping (stability/ribosome binding), 3' polyadenylation (nuclear export/stability), and splicing (intron excision by spliceosomes).

questions.question: What is 'RNA Splicing' carried out by Spliceosomes (snRNPs)?

options.A: The precision excision of non-coding intervening sequences (Introns) and joining of coding sequences (Exons)
options.B: Cutting DNA at palindromic restriction sites

questions.explanation: Introns ('intervening') are excised and exons ('expressed') are ligated together by spliceosomes to form mature translatable mRNA.

questions.question: What is the biological significance of 'Alternative RNA Splicing' in eukaryotes?

options.A: It allows a single pre-mRNA transcript to generate multiple distinct protein isoforms by selecting different combinations of exons
options.B: It increases the number of chromosomes in daughter cells
options.C: It converts messenger RNA into transfer RNA
options.D: It mutates base pairs to produce genetic diseases

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing explains how ~20,000 human genes can encode over 100,000 diverse protein isoforms across different tissues.

questions.question: How many consecutive mRNA nucleotides constitute a single 'Codon' specifying one amino acid in the genetic code?

options.A: 3 nucleotides (Triplet Code)

questions.explanation: The genetic code is a triplet code ($4^3 = 64$ codons), providing more than enough capacity to specify the 20 standard amino acids.

questions.question: What is the universal 'Start Codon' that initiates translation and specifies the amino acid Methionine?

options.A: AUG

questions.explanation: AUG is the universal start codon in mRNA, signaling the ribosomal initiator tRNA to insert formylmethionine (prokaryotes) or methionine (eukaryotes).

questions.question: Which three codons serve as 'Stop Codons' (Nonsense codons) that signal termination of protein translation?

options.A: UAA, UAG, and UGA

questions.explanation: UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), and UGA (opal) do not code for any amino acid; they bind release factors that terminate translation.

questions.question: What does it mean that the genetic code is 'Degenerate' (Redundant)?

options.A: Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon (e.g., Leucine is coded by 6 different codons)
options.B: The code breaks down rapidly at room temperature
options.C: Codons overlap with each other during reading
options.D: Different species use completely contradictory codons

questions.explanation: Degeneracy means 61 sense codons code for only 20 amino acids, buffering organisms against deleterious point mutations (silent mutations).

questions.question: What is the cloverleaf-shaped adaptor RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid at its 3' CCA-terminal and recognizes an mRNA codon via its Anticodon loop?

options.A: Transfer RNA (tRNA)

questions.explanation: tRNA translates nucleotide language into amino acid sequence by pairing its anticodon with mRNA codons while holding the appropriate amino acid.

questions.question: Which enzyme accurately couples each amino acid to its corresponding tRNA molecule, charging the tRNA in an ATP-dependent reaction?

options.A: Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase

questions.explanation: 20 aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases ensure translational fidelity by esterifying the correct amino acid to its cognate tRNA.

questions.question: Where does protein Translation take place inside eukaryotic cells?

options.A: On Ribosomes in the cytoplasm and on the rough endoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation: Translation occurs on cytoplasmic ribosomes (free or membrane-bound to the rough ER), where mRNA templates are decoded into polypeptides.

questions.question: Which catalytic activity of the large ribosomal subunit (mediated by 28S/23S rRNA as a ribozyme) forms peptide bonds between amino acids?

options.A: Peptidyl Transferase

questions.explanation: Peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme (rRNA catalytic activity) that transfers the growing polypeptide chain to the amino acid on the A-site tRNA.

questions.question: What are the three tRNA binding sites on the assembled functional ribosome during translation elongation?

options.A: A site (Aminoacyl), P site (Peptidyl), and E site (Exit)

questions.explanation: Incoming aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site; peptide bond forms at the P site; discharged uncharged tRNA exits via the E site.

questions.question: What type of gene mutation occurs when the insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides not divisible by 3 alters the entire downstream reading frame?

options.A: Frameshift Mutation

questions.explanation: Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 bases alters the triplet reading frame downstream, producing entirely different amino acids and premature stop codons.

questions.question: What is a 'Missense Mutation'?

options.A: A single nucleotide substitution that results in a codon specifying a different amino acid (e.g., Sickle Cell Anemia: GAG $\rightarrow$ GTG, Glu $\rightarrow$ Val)
options.B: A mutation that changes a codon to a premature stop codon
options.C: A mutation that produces no change in the amino acid sequence
options.D: The duplication of an entire chromosome

questions.explanation: Missense point mutations alter one codon to code for a different amino acid, altering protein folding or function (as in sickle cell disease).

questions.question: What is a 'Nonsense Mutation'?

options.A: A point mutation that changes an amino acid codon into a premature stop codon, causing truncated, non-functional protein production
options.B: A mutation that changes a codon into an identical amino acid
options.C: A mutation that multiplies the number of ribosomes

questions.explanation: Nonsense mutations introduce premature termination codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), truncating the polypeptide chain prematurely.

questions.question: In the classic Operon model of prokaryotic gene regulation (e.g., Lac Operon in E. coli), what is an 'Operator'?

options.A: A DNA regulatory sequence where a repressor protein binds to physically block RNA polymerase from transcribing structural genes
options.B: The structural gene coding for beta-galactosidase
options.C: The ribosome binding site on mRNA
options.D: A chemical inducer like lactose or allolactose

questions.explanation: The operator is a DNA segment between the promoter and structural genes where repressor binding prevents RNA polymerase transit.
